analysis.one_liner: Offers federal grants to states that require bias training for police and independent prosecution of officers' deadly force.
analysis.headline: The bill, with 12 cosponsors all Democrats or independents, was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a new federal grant program for states. To get the money, a state would have to require every police officer and academy trainee to complete yearly training on fair and impartial policing — covering bias, cultural diversity, crisis intervention, and de-escalation — and pass a state law requiring that police shootings that kill or injure someone be investigated and prosecuted by someone independent of the local department. States that do not meet the requirements would simply be ineligible for the grant money; nothing would be forced on them.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of states that opt in — especially Black and brown communities, people with disabilities, and people in mental-health crisis who are disproportionately harmed by police use of force [S2]. Communities would get officers trained annually in de-escalation and bias awareness, and police shootings would be investigated and prosecuted outside the local chain of command, addressing the conflict of interest when a department investigates its own officers [S2]. States that adopt the requirements would receive federal grant funding to implement them [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents of states that opt in

how_it_helps.text: Requires annual fair-and-impartial policing training for all officers and academy recruits — at least 8 hours initially and 4 hours each year after — covering implicit and explicit bias, cultural diversity, interaction with people with mental illness or disabilities, crisis intervention, and de-escalation, with officers tested through scenario-based exercises [S2].

Conditions federal grant money on states enacting an 'independent prosecution of law enforcement statute,' so that any police use of deadly force causing death or injury is investigated and prosecuted by a civilian review board, the state attorney general, a special prosecutor, an outside agency, or an independent prosecutor from outside the county — not the officer's own department [S2].
Includes verification and audit safeguards: state attorneys general must verify compliance and the Justice Department's Inspector General would audit states receiving the grants each year [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would fund the grants; states that opt in would bear the cost of delivering yearly training to all officers and recruits and of running independent investigation and prosecution procedures, offset by the federal grant [S2]. Police departments in participating states would give up the practice of having their own agencies investigate their officers' shootings [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers and opt-in state governments

drawbacks.text: The bill is entirely voluntary: a state with poor policing practices can simply decline the grant and face no requirement at all, so the worst-performing states face no pressure to change [S2].
The bill text contains no dedicated appropriation for the grants, so the money would depend on future congressional funding decisions [S2].

The definition of 'independent prosecution' is flexible enough to allow investigation by another law enforcement agency under a memorandum of understanding, an arrangement critics of the same approach argue is not truly independent because outside agencies often work closely with the department under review [S2].

Yearly training for every officer in a state, plus independent investigation of every deadly-force incident causing death or injury, would impose real administrative and staffing costs on state and local governments in participating states [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For states that opt in, the bill pairs a concrete benefit — federal money — with reforms that civil-rights groups have long sought: regular de-escalation and bias training and taking deadly-force prosecutions out of the hands of the officer's own colleagues. The main weakness is design rather than cost: because participation is voluntary and no money is specifically appropriated, the bill would have reached only willing states and might have funded few of them. The training costs fall on participating states but are meant to be offset by the grants.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in late July 2024, referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and sat there without a hearing, a vote, or any further action until the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Tammy Duckworth introduced the bill on July 30, 2024, joined by 12 original cosponsors — 11 Senate Democrats and Senator Bernie Sanders, the chamber's only Independent caucusing with Democrats [S1] [S3] [S4].
That same day the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee, which was its last action of any kind [S4].
The Judiciary Committee never held a markup or hearing on the bill and the full Senate never considered it; the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No reform resulted, so the outcome left state law-enforcement practices and the status quo of departments investigating their own officers' shootings untouched. States were spared any new training or prosecution requirements, and federal money that would have gone to the grant program was never spent.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo; no reform, no new mandates

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, but all 12 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's independent, and no Republican sponsored it, so any fight over it would almost certainly have split by party.

industries.industry: State and local law enforcement agencies
industries.note: In states that take the grant, every department would have to deliver yearly bias, de-escalation, and crisis-intervention training, and deadly-force cases would move to outside investigators and prosecutors instead of the department's own chain of command. Because participation is voluntary, agencies in unwilling states would feel no effect.

Independent prosecution statutes of the kind the bill incentivizes typically weaken unions' ability to keep deadly-force cases within friendly local prosecutors' offices; the record contains no direct union position on this bill.
Opt-in states would receive new federal grant money and DOJ audit-backed support for training and independent prosecution systems they might otherwise fund themselves.
